The current solution, the WLCG production system, is stretched to the limit. To address these issues, the CERN CCG has developed a new concept, CRAFT, designed to maximize computing and storage resources' full utilization, prioritize tasks adaptively, and ensure timely completion of critical analysis jobs. CRAFT's core components are modular, scalable, and designed to be integrated into the WLCG production system. Its first implementation aims to increase the running time of ATLAS analysis jobs by 2.8 times through enhanced computing capacity and improved scheduling. A more in-depth evaluation of CRAFT's potential will be conducted in future studies. CRAFT's second phase involves developing an advanced AI-driven system for optimizing data analysis workflows, capable of identifying bottlenecks and optimizing job placement to minimize overall analysis times. We investigate magnetic Raman scattering in the Haldane state, focusing on the behavior of the spin excitation. Our analysis reveals that conventional magnetic Raman scattering occurs when the frequency of the pump laser and the Stokes laser satisfies a specific condition, resulting in a mode that is a combination of two spin-flip excitations. However, when the frequency of the pump laser and the Stokes laser does not satisfy this condition, the resulting mode is unconventional and characterized by a significant amount of interband mixing. Our findings also indicate that unconventional magnetic Raman scattering is more pronounced in systems with a higher degree of interband mixing. Additionally, we have developed a method to selectively filter out conventional magnetic Raman scattering signals, allowing unconventional magnetic Raman scattering signals to be more clearly detected. Our analysis of the Haldane state in one-dimensional antiferromagnetic chains and the spin-3/2 Heisenberg model provides a foundation for understanding the behavior of spin excitations in this context. Recent studies have found that larger transformer-based language models produce less accurate surprisal estimates on various tasks, including reading time predictions. We investigate a potential explanation for this discrepancy by analyzing how these models interact with named entities in texts. We discovered that larger models tend to overestimate reading time for the prefix of a sentence containing a named entity, while underestimating the post-named entity prefix, suggesting an inaccuracy in processing entity names. We demonstrated this by training models on data with artificially introduced noise in entity names and observing a correlation between model performance and the presence of this anomaly. The results highlight a critical area of improvement for neural network-based parsing models, emphasizing the need for more robust entity handling. The rapid evolution of cyber threats has outpaced the development of effective detection tools, enabling hackers to bypass security systems with ease. This research aims to address the challenge of identifying these sophisticated attacks, which often involve the use of legitimate communication channels to evade detection, through the creation of an innovative concept known as "communication complexity profiling." By analyzing the intricacies of an organization's interactions and cross-referencing them against a database of known attacks, our proposed method offers a viable solution for quickly identifying threat sources within complex communication networks. Additionally, our research presents a cutting-edge machine learning-based approach for categorizing these threats and determining the most effective course of action to contain them. Our findings are demonstrated through the application of real-world data from two distinct industries, showcasing the effectiveness of this proposed method. Furthermore, our approach is compared to two alternative techniques to validate its accuracy and effectiveness. By leveraging advanced machine learning and deep learning models, such as Convolutional Neural Networks and Support Vector Machines, our research provides a data-driven framework for detecting and responding to modern advanced threats. The proposed solution has the potential to be integrated into existing security architectures to provide an additional layer of threat detection and incident response. The Sentinel Project, initiated by the European Space Agency, launched a series of satellites to provide global Earth observation datasets, which have gained significant adoption across various sectors. The aim of this research is to explore the use of Sentinel data in studying the impact of COVID-19 on the environment and the recovery process that follows. We analyzed the effects of COVID-19 by examining changes in nitrogen levels, re-synthesized aerosol data, and the carbon content of aerosols over Europe and China. Additionally, we utilized the Leaf-Area Index to estimate the impact of COVID-19 on the forestry industry. The results show that, in contrast to our expectations, we found no significant indication of long-term environmental recovery after the end of the lockdown periods in both Europe and China. This study provides a framework for future research on environmental recovery following the COVID-19 pandemic, and the accompanying code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/earthels/COVID-19-Environmental-Recovery. The code is intended to facilitate the use of this research in other settings and the analysis of additional locations. Consequently, we urge researchers to consider the sustainability and responsible use of resources, such as computing power and energy, as we move forward. Locating tables, charts, images, and formulas within documents can be a time-consuming process, especially when dealing with large collections of unindexed papers. To address this challenge, we developed GraphletRank, a novel query-focused approach for identifying relevant table, chart, image, and formula elements within a document. By first extracting graphical elements and converting them into a graph structure, we can then employ GraphletRank to rank these elements based on their connection to the query phrase. The GraphletRank algorithm uses a ranking function trained on query-graph interactions and has been successfully tested on an existing dataset, achieving substantial time improvements in retrieving specific graphical elements when compared to standard approaches. Furthermore, our method's effectiveness is further validated by the substantial improvement in MRR and P@10 scores achieved after integrating GraphletRank into an existing retrieval system. GraphletRank's source code is now available for public use at https://github.com/chen-jiabao/graphlet-rank. We also provide an interactive demo at https://graphlet-rank.cs.umc.edu/. Our research contributes a new graph-based solution for retrieving graphical elements within an existing retrieval system, and we propose the development of a new dataset featuring graphical queries to further support this field. The GraphletRank algorithm is also adapted to support the development of a search interface for an online repository of scientific publications at https://www.scihero.org/. This website allows users to search for tables, images, and formulas using graphical elements, such as a table of contents page or a specific chart, and provides results that are ranked by relevance to the query. The GraphletRank algorithm is now part of the CiteOrchard project, which aims to revolutionize the way we search for scientific information presented in visual formats. The emergence of deep learning has significantly enhanced the performance of child activity recognition (CAR), a vital application in monitoring the development and well-being of children. Recent CAR research has predominantly focused on image and video analysis through convolutional neural networks (CNN) and recurrent deep neural networks (RNN), such as Long-Short Term Memory (LSTM). However, these traditional methods are often limited by their failure to capture the complex temporal and spatial relationships within child activities. To address this limitation, researchers have turned to graph convolution networks (GCN), which are well-suited to modeling complex relationships. A CAR system that integrates GCN with temporal information, dubbed TempGCN, is proposed in this paper. TempGCN leverages the spatio-temporal relationships within child activities by encoding temporal information into graph structures and utilizing GCN for node feature extraction. The proposed method is evaluated using the NIST Kids' Safe Human Action Dataset and demonstrated to outperform state-of-the-art CAR models, including those based on CNN and RNN. The proposed method is validated through ablation experiments, and the code is made available for further research. The study's findings are expected to stimulate further innovation in deep learning-based child action recognition techniques. This approach is applied to solve the Fokker-Planck equation in the solvable quantum harmonic oscillator system. The derived solutions are compared with actual simulations of the system, and the impact of the non-stationary drift on the underlying phase space dynamics is examined. The underlying mechanism of over-parameterization in machine learning models has been found to contribute significantly to their generalizability. This phenomenon is further investigated within the context of adversarial robustness in shallow neural networks. Our study reveals that over-parameterization does not necessarily lead to robust optimization, and in fact, it may even hinder the optimization process for certain adversarial robustness constraints. Through theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that the optimal trade-off between model complexity and accuracy/robustness is influenced by the specific problem at hand. Notably, in problems where the number of parameters grows sub-linearly with the number of inputs, the optimization of adversarial robustness is significantly facilitated, whereas in problems where the number of parameters grows at a linear rate, the optimization is severely impaired. Our findings are supported by empirical evidence. Additionally, our study provides new insights into the effect of over-parameterization on adversarial robustness and sheds light on the role of over-parameterization in facilitating generalization. These results are expected to be relevant to deeper networks and to provide a better understanding of adversarial robustness in general. By incorporating a compact feature descriptor, our algorithm minimizes processing requirements, making it suitable for real-time implementation. Additionally, a robust ranking system is introduced to filter out false positives, enhancing overall efficiency. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed solution achieves faster computation times without compromising accuracy, outperforming existing loop closure detection techniques. Notably, the bi-directional approach also outperforms a traditional one-way approach, achieving a 10% improvement in recall and 5% in precision during autonomous navigation. Further improvements in accuracy and efficiency are achieved through the incorporation of a ranking system, increasing precision to 99% and reducing false positives by 20% compared to the bi-directional approach alone. Moreover, the proposed feature descriptor exhibits superior performance, demonstrating 20% more recalls and 5% more precision in detecting identical trajectories compared to traditional methods. Finally, the contribution of the ranking system to overall performance is also highlighted, showing a 20% more precise output and 20% fewer false positives. A crucial component of quantum computing is quantum compiling, which creates a set of quantum gates from a given sequence. This paper introduces a new, modified version of the genetic algorithm tailored to quantum compiling. Differing from the traditional algorithm, which focuses on gate count, this variant aims to minimize errors in quantum circuits. To assess the performance of the algorithm, we used the fidelity figure of merit to evaluate its effectiveness. A notable advantage of this approach is its ability to achieve a near-optimal set of gates after only 10 iterations, surpassing even the best known genetic algorithms. Furthermore, the results show that the final quantum circuit after 10 iterations has an error rate of 0.03 or less, indicating its high quality. This improved genetic algorithm also outperforms other quantum compiling methods and serves as a useful tool for future research. To demonstrate its capabilities, we successfully implemented the modified genetic algorithm to compile the quantum circuit for the Bernstein-Vazirani algorithm. This success paves the way for the application of this variant to other quantum algorithms and promises to enhance performance. To facilitate further research, the code used in this study has been made available online. Additionally, the work has been extended to compile quantum circuits for other algorithms such as Grover's algorithm and quantum teleportation, and the results show promising outcomes. Finally, the modified genetic algorithm has been applied to compile quantum circuits for basic operations including the Hadamard gate, Pauli gates, and the phase gate, and the results show that it achieves near-optimal error rates of 0.01 or less after just 10 iterations. Recent advancements in unsupervised reinforcement learning have led to significant improvements in task adaptation, enabling agents to learn from limited task labels. A notable example is the open-source master version of DART, a system capable of adapting to new tasks with minimal supervision. This paper builds upon DART, introducing an enhanced framework, referred to as Adaptive Reinforcement Learning from Demonstrations (ARLD). A key component of ARLD is its use of a task-conditioned latent space to support the development of a single policy that can perform well across multiple tasks. Additionally, ARLD leverages a task-conditioned loss function to guide task learning and provides task-specific fine-tuning to ensure effective task adaptation. Experimental evaluations of ARLD on a variety of continuous control environments demonstrate its ability to learn new tasks efficiently from limited labels, outperforming existing benchmarks. Furthermore, ARLD's analysis of task adaptation reveals insights into its behavior and identifies areas for potential improvement. As a result, ARLD offers a promising approach to unsupervised transfer learning, warranting further investigation. Recent studies have highlighted the discrepancies between self-supervised and fully supervised contrastive learning methods. In response, we've developed a new metric called Smoothness of Representation Manifold (SRM), which assesses the smoothness of the representation space generated by these models. Our findings indicate that the SRM values for self-supervised methods are often higher, suggesting more natural representation variations. Notably, we've observed that self-supervised models can successfully capture the SRM of fully supervised models, achieving comparable performance on downstream tasks. Furthermore, we've found that augmentations that work well for self-supervised models can be effectively applied to fully supervised models during fine-tuning, leading to significant speedups in training time. Overall, our research demonstrates that self-supervised models can be designed to produce smooth representation spaces and excel in downstream tasks. Moreover, we've established a new application for self-supervised models, namely, improving the smoothness of fully supervised models. This study focuses on the asymptotic properties of the spatial integral of the parabolic Anderson model on an n-dimensional torus, with time approaching infinity. The model's noise component is driven by a Gaussian process whose covariance function decays at a polynomial rate, specifically, its magnitude decreases at a $\rho$ degree, where $\rho$ is a positive integer. We derive an expression for the asymptotic behavior of the time integral based on the local time of the process at a specific point. This result is achieved by establishing a local time representation formula for the process and demonstrating that the point at which the process is evaluated has a substantial impact on the overall behavior of the process, particularly, its typical behavior is dictated by the point at which the process attains its maximum. Our findings extend previous research conducted by Gao and Zhang for the one-dimensional case and include sharp error estimates. Additionally, our research reveals that the polynomial rate of decay in the covariance function has a significant effect on the local time and, consequently, on the asymptotic behavior of the time integral. In theories of technicolor, the self-coupling of the Higgs boson is linked to the technicolor symmetry breaking scale. This connection is strengthened by the use of technifermions in these theories, particularly those with multiple technigenerations. Our research focuses on a non-minimal technicolor framework, where a single technigeneration model is generalized by introducing additional technicolors and multiple techni-quark pairs. This "minimally minimal" framework allows for a more precise analysis of how techni-Higgs couplings to Standard Model fermions are affected, providing a first-principles derivation of the one-loop renormalization group equations governing the theory. Our results show that, in this model, the techni-Higgs couplings to Standard Model fermions are not significantly enhanced, leading to a stronger link between the Higgs self-coupling and the technicolor symmetry breaking scale than in models with multiple technigenerations. This is particularly relevant for theories where the symmetry breaking scale is very high, resulting in a large self-coupling of the Higgs boson. Our research also explores the implications of these findings for the direct production of Higgs bosons at the Large Hadron Collider. Specifically, we find that, in this model, the production rates for Higgs boson pairs through gluon-gluon fusion are significantly higher than in the Standard Model, leading to a potential discovery opportunity at the LHC with a 5σ significance at a 300 fb-1 luminosity. Our results also indicate that, in this model, the production of Higgs boson pairs through vector-boson fusion is not as significant as in the Standard Model, leading to a potential discovery opportunity primarily through gluon-gluon fusion. Our research also discusses the implications of these findings for the production of Higgs bosons on the electroweak precision constraints imposed by the LEP data, finding that these constraints are more stringent in our model than in models with multiple technigenerations. By leveraging the solvability of Hermitian Calogero-Sutherland systems, we successfully adapt these solutions to non-Hermitian contexts, employing a transformation approach. Our findings reveal a range of new solvable models with intricate spectral patterns, including systems featuring real spectrum gaps and alternating real and complex energy levels and eigenvalues. Furthermore, we examine the implications of these discoveries and identify potential avenues for future investigation. Moreover, we successfully apply our method to non-Hermitian Calogero-Moser systems and non-Hermitian Chaly-Sutherland models, resulting in the derivation of explicit resonances. Lastly, we explore the connection between our work and prior research on non-Hermitian systems featuring real spectrum gaps and exceptional points. Our studies demonstrate that these exceptional points consistently correspond to real spectrum gaps in our models, and we speculate that this relationship may hold more general significance. Machine learning models are often susceptible to noise in data, which can cause them to underperform in real-world applications. A particular type of noise, known as label noise, occurs when the true labels assigned by a cost function do not always match the actual labels. In this paper, we investigate the effects of noise on the training of neural networks when classifying handwritten digits using the MNIST dataset. We find that the influence of noise can vary depending on the network architecture, with deeper networks generally being more resistant to it. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the introduction of noise can lead to the formation of sub-optimal local minima in the loss landscape, which can hinder the training process. To mitigate this issue, we suggest a simple approach that involves re-classifying data points with high uncertainty, which we achieve by introducing dropouts during training. This approach not only helps to reduce the negative impact of noise but also leads to the discovery of novel network configurations that are more resilient to noise, thereby improving the overall performance of the model. Ultimately, our results suggest that the application of simple and robust training methods can yield significant gains in performance, even when the model is trained with noisy labels. The Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture has shown great promise in scaling up deep learning models, allowing for efficient parallelization on large-scale accelerators. To address this issue, we introduce a novel approach, called Gating Dropout (GDU), which employs dropout techniques to randomize gate bias and promote more even token utilization. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of GDU in enhancing model performance, particularly in scenarios with biased gate layers, and show that it can be seamlessly integrated into various MoE architectures. Experimental results across multiple datasets and settings confirm that GDU can significantly improve token utilization efficiency, leading to faster and more efficient training processes. Additionally, we demonstrate the scalability of GDU on large-scale datasets and accelerators, making it a promising solution for real-world applications. The Gamma-Ray Energy Tracking Array (GRETA), comprising a series of highly specialized detectors, is tailored for tracking gamma-rays in experiments involving electron-positron collisions at lepton colliders. Each detector has an exceptionally high efficiency in detecting gamma-rays, thereby enabling the precise measurement of electron energies in collisions. In the current design, detectors feature thin scintillator layers and silicon photomultipliers wrapped in active plastic fibers. We have developed a simulation model, utilizing GEANT4, to predict the detection efficiency of these detectors. Our results indicate that with the current design, detection efficiency would only reach 65% of the maximum theoretical value, primarily due to the non-uniformity of silicon photomultipliers and active plastic fibers. To enhance detection efficiency, we propose a simplified design for the scintillator layers, replacing the wrapped fibers with end-fibers connected to a single photomultiplier. Our revised efficiency estimates indicate that this modified design achieves 95% of the maximum detection potential. Additionally, we have calculated the angular resolution for gamma-rays in collisions, showing that it improves significantly with increasing gamma-ray energies. For a 5-GeV gamma-ray, the angular resolution is approximately 2.5 milliradians, while for a 100-GeV gamma-ray, the angular resolution is significantly improved, reaching 0.2 milliradians. Overall, our revised design offers a superior balance of detection efficiency and angular resolution at lower gamma-ray energies. We have also explored the feasibility of using specialized detectors, like silicon PMTs and SiPM arrays, in place of the current silicon photomultipliers. Our results indicate that these alternative detectors can match or exceed the performance of the current photomultipliers, thereby enabling the precise tracking of electron energies in collisions. Finally, we have developed a simulation model for the tracking of electron energies in collisions using a single detector. Our results indicate that this model can accurately predict the electron energy with a resolution of 0.5% at low energies and 0.1% at high energies. We have also investigated the feasibility of using this model to predict the electron energy spectrum in collisions, including the detection of low-energy electrons produced in the electron-positron collision process. Our results indicate that this model can accurately capture the electron energy spectrum in the final state of collisions, including the detection of low-energy electrons. As deep learning models become increasingly prevalent in sensitive domains, such as healthcare, the need to protect training data from unauthorized access has become a pressing concern. Despite this, the effectiveness of privacy-enhancing techniques in training data has not been thoroughly explored, particularly when employing convolutional neural networks. This study investigates the impact of leveraging pre-trained CNN models on data privacy, utilizing a de-identification metric, and finds that such models pose a significant risk of revealing sensitive training data even after undergoing quantization. Furthermore, the findings suggest that combining multiple models to make a prediction can actually compromise privacy, rather than improve it. This research aims to raise awareness about the potential risks associated with using CNN-based models to protect training data privacy. In a theoretical framework inspired by higher dimensional theories such as Weyl-Yang-Kaluza-Klein gravity and 5D theories, a massive graviton model with two tensor fields in four-dimensional Minkowski spacetime is formulated. The model is based on a non-minimal coupling between the tensor fields and the metric that mimics the interaction between the Weyl connection and the scalar field in 5D theories. The model's equations of motion are derived, and massive graviton solutions are obtained using a generalized wave propagation equation. The presence of both gravitational and gravitational-like waves in the model is demonstrated. The study also examines the stability of massive gravitons in the model. The abstract concludes by highlighting the potential for a more general framework that could result from this theoretical work. The full text of this theoretical framework will be presented in a companion paper.

However, it faces a significant challenge in achieving high accuracy, particularly when working with non-identically distributed data sets. To address this issue, we introduce a novel online federated learning framework that incorporates multiple kernel-based techniques. Building upon the foundation of online multiple kernel learning, we extend it to the federated setting while also considering the non-IID data challenge. The key advantage of our approach lies in its ability to learn individualized kernel functions for each client, thus mitigating the effects of non-IID data. Theoretical analysis reveals that our MK-OFL algorithm enjoys optimal generalization error bounds, comparable to those achieved by OMKL in the i.i.d. setting. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our approach outperforms a naive extension of OMKL in the non-IID setting. The efficacy of our framework is also validated through a series of experiments conducted on both synthetic and real-world data sets. The experiments reveal that our MK-OFL algorithm outperforms several baseline methods, including FedAvg and FedMKL, in terms of convergence speed and accuracy. We examine multiple polylogarithms from an algebraic perspective, by developing a method to express them in terms of holomorphic 1-forms on a universal abelian cover of the polylogarithm's defining domain. This formulation enables us to study the multiple polylogarithm's properties as a Rota-Baxter algebra, including its cohomology, and reveals the unit and associativity relations specifically represent coboundaries in our algebraic framework. A corresponding universal algebraic structure is identified, and its generators are shown to correspond to 1-dimensional cohomology classes within this algebraic context. Furthermore, our approach allows us to calculate the Chevalley-Eilenberg complex of the multiple polylogarithm's 1-forms and determine its 1-dimensional cohomology, and we also derive a universal central extension of the free Lie algebra generated by these forms. Additionally, we introduce and study the properties of a generalised Goncharov polylogarithm by mapping it to cohomology classes within this algebraic context. Finally, we extend our analysis to quantum multiple polylogarithms by demonstrating that these can be expressed as a specific type of 1-form on an extended domain, and we calculate their corresponding cohomology and 1-dimensional cohomology classes. A corresponding universal central extension of the free Lie algebra generated by these classes is identified and studied. In the past decade, researchers in computational social sciences have developed novel approaches for text analysis and emotion detection, leveraging large datasets of historical data to uncover new insights. This research employs a unique dataset of nearly 20 million tweets related to the Australian federal election to identify and quantify emotions associated with political parties and topics. Our findings indicate a notable shift in media reporting from 2007 to 2019, with increased focus on key issues like asylum policy and climate change. Notably, our data analysis reveals a higher incidence of positive and negative emotions in Labor Party-related tweets compared to those for the Liberal Party. This disparity is most pronounced in discussions of asylum policy, where discussions often centered on concerns about refugee numbers, security risks, and the screening process. Our study also uncovers distinct linguistic patterns in external news sources, with the Liberal Party being more likely to focus on economic matters and the Labor Party to focus on social welfare issues. Finally, our data analysis reveals a correlation between the tone of tweets and media reporting, with negative sentiments in both often emerging in response to key issues like asylum policy and crime. This study provides valuable insights for social scientists, journalists, and political analysts alike, offering a nuanced understanding of public sentiment and media reporting during the Australian federal election. Our findings can inform effective strategies for improving public sentiment and media reporting, making them an invaluable resource for political parties seeking to shape the tone of the national conversation. Self-supervised learning methods, such as SimCLR and BYOL, have garnered significant attention by leveraging contrastive learning to learn visual representations from unlabeled data.  These approaches typically involve designing a model to solve two tasks simultaneously, but our research reveals that incorporating explicit information compression through a technique called contrastive distillation enhances their performance.  We introduce a novel self-supervised learning framework called DistSim, which combines two distinct principles: maximizing mutual information and minimizing the difference between the original data and its distilled form.  DistSim outperforms SimCLR in the CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and ImageNet-100 datasets, achieving notable improvements of 3%, 4.5%, and 2% respectively in the absence of any class balance considerations.  Moreover, when applied to ImageNet-1k, DistSim surpasses SimCLR's state-of-the-art performance by a substantial margin of 1.2% in the linear evaluation setting.  Our findings demonstrate the benefits of incorporating information compression into self-supervised learning approaches.  The code and models for DistSim are publicly available on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/alexandriabai/DistSim.  Furthermore, we also present DistSim++ - a variant of DistSim that incorporates a multi-teacher architecture, which achieves even higher state-of-the-art results on the CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and ImageNet-100 datasets.  The code for Dist++ is publicly available on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/alexandriabai/Dist++/.  Both frameworks are designed to be modular and can be easily adapted to various existing self-supervised learning methods. We have developed a novel tree-based decoder designed specifically for 
programming languages, drawing on the grammar rules to guide the translation
process. Unlike previous decoders that focus solely on the syntax tree and 
ignore programming logic, our decoder uses the syntax tree as input and 
integrates grammar rules to generate coherent code. This approach allows 
our model to produce high-quality code, as evidenced by the fact that it was 
able to pass all tests for the provided programming challenges without any 
errors. Furthermore, we observed that our decoder outperformed a context-based 
decoder model that was trained with more data. In addition, we leveraged 
multilingual capabilities to utilize a Spanish speaker in the translation 
process, resulting in a significant 50% improvement in the BLEU score. To 
further enhance our model's capabilities, we employed a semi-supervised 
approach known as pseudo-labeling. Interestingly, our results demonstrate 
significant improvements in the BLEU score as the number of pseudo-labels 
increases, ultimately leading to a 300% increase in the optimal model settings. 
In a surprising twist, we found that our decoder's performance was influenced 
by the programming language used for the syntax tree as well as the target 
programming language. Specifically, our model performed significantly 
better when translating from Python to Java than when translating from Python to 
C. This suggests that our model is able to capture the unique logic and 
conventions of a programming language, allowing it to produce more accurate 
and maintainable code. In conclusion, our results highlight the potential of 
using the syntax tree and grammar rules in code generation, and we believe that

This study outlines the development process for an open-source speaker verification system. Notably, our study found that Word2Vec features outperformed conventional features in some instances, highlighting their potential as reliable AD biomarkers. Federated Reinforcement Learning (FRL) is an emerging area of machine learning that enables agents to learn cooperative behaviors through direct interaction with their environment, despite being located in disparate states. FRL is distinguished from traditional Federated Learning by its reliance on reinforcement learning algorithms that operate in line with environmental dynamics. This has led to a proliferation of novel FRL algorithms, which can be categorized based on the distribution of agents into centralized and decentralized systems. Centralized FRL systems involve a central learning hub that aggregates data from multiple agents, while decentralized FRL systems utilize local learning and communication protocols to facilitate learning. Despite considerable attention to FRL, there is a lack of a unified review of the underlying principles and methodologies. This paper aims to bridge this gap by providing an in-depth examination of FRL systems, highlighting the key differences between centralized and decentralized approaches and their respective advantages and limitations. Furthermore, it discusses the challenges associated with FRL, including issues related to privacy, security, and communication, and outlines potential future research directions in the field. This paper is intended to serve as a comprehensive resource for researchers and practitioners seeking to understand the capabilities and applications of FRL in decentralized learning environments. It is anticipated that FRL will continue to play a significant role in the development of decentralized learning systems in the future. We introduce Choice Trees (ctrees), an extension of regular trees that effectively models complex, uncertain programming scenarios. By merging path concatenation and branching operations, ctrees enable a unified representation of both regular and recursive functions. The resulting concept of ctrees offers a robust framework for analyzing and reasoning about probabilistic programs. Most notably, we establish that ctrees can accurately model stochastic functions with a level of precision equivalent to a specific probability measure. Furthermore, we establish a rigorous method for analyzing the complexity of ctrees and show that their size can be bounded by a certain threshold when derived from recursive functions. Finally, we explore the practical implications of our approach and identify key challenges for future research. As a demonstration of its practicality, we showcase the application of ctrees in representing probabilistic function schemes and outline the benefits of using ctrees to model stochastic functions within programming languages. Mobile robots designed to operate in areas where humans are present must be able to safely coexist and accomplish tasks together. To achieve this goal, these robots need to navigate through crowded spaces without interfering with or harming humans, while also completing their assigned tasks efficiently. In order to better understand how to enable collaborative robot navigation, we developed a computational model that simulates human-robot interaction using the concept of empowerment. Our model suggests that a robot's ability to take control of its environment can influence human behavior in shared work areas, leading to either cooperative or competitive interactions. Using this model, we created a virtual reality environment where humans and robots work together, involving the robot performing a time-critical task while avoiding obstacles, similar to a typical first-person video game. Our experiments showed that when robots are more empowered, humans tend to be more cooperative and assist the robot by moving out of its path. In contrast, less empowered robots are more likely to be helped by humans in order to avoid collisions. Our findings indicate that robot empowerment can be a crucial factor in optimizing human-robot collaboration. The data and resources from our study are available online for further research. Future investigations can explore how different control methods, such as reinforcement learning, affect robot empowerment and its impact on human behavior in shared workspaces. This knowledge may help develop more effective and efficient robot control systems that benefit both humans and robots. In the long run, our research could lead to the creation of more harmonious and collaborative robotic systems. Our results show that the HSP method is capable of producing high-quality resampled data sets with reduced noise and improved accuracy. In the field of recommendation systems, a common practice is to display a curated list of the most appealing items alongside additional suggestions categorized by their predicted appeal levels. While this approach may seem beneficial by showcasing top choices alongside varying degrees of matches, it can lead to several issues. First, it may cause users to overlook valuable, yet lower-ranked suggestions for which they would pay premium. Secondly, it may result in a less-than-ideal list by mixing and mismatching items based on their predicted appeal levels. We propose a novel method called FairMix to address these concerns by creating a single, cohesive list that both promotes fairness and accuracy. FairMix is an optimization technique that tackles a complex problem by ensuring a predetermined number of highly appealing items are included in the top part of the list while the lower part is populated by a different set of items based on a fairness constraint. We demonstrate that FairMix is a non-linear optimization problem and develop a solution that iteratively updates a binary representation of the items in the list, along with a secondary objective to optimize the list's accuracy. We demonstrate FairMix outperforms existing approaches in terms of both fairness and accuracy. We also show that FairMix can be easily adapted to work with various data types, including text and images. To support our claims, we conducted extensive experiments on real-world datasets, highlighting the effectiveness of FairMix in addressing the issues with the current standard practice. In a massive network of interacting parties with diverse views, communication among voters is influenced by the news they consume. A crucial aspect of our model reveals that echo chambers emerge naturally when parties have varied preferences and voters are exposed to multiple sources of information. To prevent the creation of these isolated structures, both of which can impede party alignment, individuals must be diverse in the news they consume. Interestingly, a significant cost is associated with party victory when parties with distinct views form their own chambers, and this cost can be significantly reduced if voters are allowed to choose from a diverse set of news sources. This research expands upon previous studies that considered only polynomial nonlinearity on bounded domains. In contrast, our findings allow for more general, non-Lipschitz nonlinearities, such as those derived from the integration of $e^{-|x|^\alpha}$, where $\alpha$ is greater than one, thereby mirroring the scenario on the entire Euclidean space. Notably, our solutions exhibit temporal continuity and satisfy the given wave equation in a distributional sense but do not fulfill the classical conditions. These findings are derived from a representation of the solution in an integral form, featuring time-dependent kernels, which can be expressed through an iterated Stieltjes integral. Furthermore, we establish a representation of the solution in terms of a Volterra type integral involving a kernel with a non-Lipschitz behavior. The discovery of Meltdown and Spectre in 2017 highlighted the need for comprehensive test suites in evaluating processor security. Although some initiatives have been launched to develop test suites for these vulnerabilities, they currently fall short in essential properties, such as thorough coverage and precise location identification, and are often limited to specific use cases. To address this, we introduce a novel test suite called PUMA, designed to target the Side Channels of Meltdown and SpectA, a collective term for L1 Terminal Block attacks. By utilizing a program analysis approach, PUMA generates tests that cover 99% of the vulnerable L1T code and 100% of the vulnerable L1B code, and pinpoints the exact locations of the Side Channel vulnerabilities. The tests developed by PUMA are not only efficient in terms of time and memory usage but also outperform existing tests in terms of code coverage. Furthermore, PUMA's precision in locating the Side Channel vulnerabilities makes it an effective tool for code review. monitored by these devices. The increasing number of connected homes has enabled
smart metering, allowing utility companies to track energy usage in real-time.
This research aims to address the challenges of security and privacy by proposing
an innovative blockchain-based framework, which utilizes IoT networks to manage
sub-metering systems and ensure user privacy. The proposed framework incorporates
a novel consensus mechanism, coupled with advanced filtering techniques, to effectively
manage IoT data and prevent unauthorized access. The framework's validity is
demonstrated through a case study, theoretical metrics are identified, and key
performance indicators are proposed to evaluate the feasibility of the designed
solution. The proposed blockchain-based IoT framework is anticipated to enhance IoT
security and user privacy, providing a secure environment for future IoT development. 
This research is part of the ongoing work on the IoT ecosystem, aiming to address
the pressing issues of security, privacy, and blockchain-based IoT networks. 
Future research will focus on further optimizing and refining the proposed
framework.

The widespread adoption of machine-to-machine (S) and machine-to-machine (C) communication devices is expected to surge in the near future, with these devices projected to surpass human usage according to certain forecasts. A significant challenge arises in this context, as the diverse range of S-C applications will present a complex problem for future 5G networks, particularly in terms of managing machine-to-device communication. Existing studies have primarily focused on resolving the issue of non-terrestrial networks, but the problem of managing M2M communications in complex environments will be explored in this paper. Specifically, this paper will investigate the optimal placement of access points in urban settings, taking into account the unique characteristics of M2M communication devices, such as device isolation requirements and varying communication requirements. A novel hybrid placement algorithm will be proposed, combining the strengths of fractal and fractal subdivision methods to achieve an optimal balance of coverage, device isolation, and energy efficiency. The algorithm's performance will be validated through simulation results. The findings in this paper are intended to provide valuable insights and practical guidelines for future 5G network researchers and practitioners. Moreover, this work aims to contribute to the development of M2M communication solutions tailored to diverse settings, such as urban, rural, and industrial environments. The paper's conclusions and potential future research directions will also be discussed. Lastly, this work is intended as a stepping stone for further research in this field. The goal of image restoration is to recover a noise-free image from a corrupted observation, yet existing datasets are plagued by images with extreme noise levels that make effective training models. To address this challenge, we developed a new concept, image restoration potential, which assesses the potential difficulty of restoring noise-affected images. Based on this approach, we introduce Image Restoration Difficulty (IRD), a metric to quantify the restoration complexity of images. Utilizing IRD, we have created a selection of training images with optimal levels of noise, dubbed as Easy-Noises, which significantly enhance the performance of image restoration models. Specifically, our proposed model achieves a notable 1.5 dB improvement over the state-of-the-art methods when trained on Easy-Noises, resulting in a superior performance on ImageNet, DIV2K, and BSD64. The source code for the project is publicly available at https://github.com/THU-CyberSec/erd. Our research findings contribute to the field of image restoration by providing a new evaluation metric and a comprehensive understanding of restoration complexity. The Easy-Noises dataset, used in our experiments, is also made available for the research community to utilize. This work has the potential to significantly enhance the performance of image restoration models, enabling them to handle challenging noise levels that previously hindered their performance. Ultimately, our research provides a new perspective on image restoration and offers a novel approach to training models for this critical task. With the availability of Easy-Noises, we believe that this breakthrough will significantly advance the state-of-the-art in image restoration and open up new avenues of research in this field. A robust steering controller is designed to ensure the robot's stability and accuracy in crowded environments. The proposed framework is tested through simulations of complex scenarios, demonstrating its effectiveness in navigating dense obstacles. The presented work paves the way for the development of practical human-robot teaming systems for guiding aerial robots in dynamic environments. This study introduces a cutting-edge visual speech recognition system that utilizes transfer learning and deep convolutional neural networks to analyze facial expressions and recognize emotional speech. By leveraging a pre-trained model for facial action recognition, we demonstrate the effectiveness of transfer learning in significantly enhancing emotional speech recognition accuracy. We also explore the potential for transfer learning when employing facial action recognition as an intermediate step to facilitate emotional speech recognition. Additionally, we demonstrate that using a pre-trained facial action recognition model as a feature extractor enables our system to achieve top-notch performance on the most challenging emotional speech dataset available. We also investigate the impact of various neural network architectures and training methods on the performance of our system, providing valuable insights for future research. Finally, we validate our findings by demonstrating the system's real-world applicability through a user simulation experiment. The results show that our system can effectively recognize emotional speech in real-time, even when the speaker is partially occluded, and can facilitate natural human-computer interaction. Estimating heart rates from video streams has numerous applications, such as surveillance, intensive care units, and public safety. A new, highly accurate algorithm for heart rate estimation is introduced, which is capable of performing globally in different settings and environments. By leveraging a combination of deep learning and optical flow, it can effectively track the head's motion and synthesize heart rate information. A novel approach to data processing is also proposed, utilizing a temporal convolutional network to analyze video frames and minimize the impact of visual disturbances. Two new datasets were created to test the proposed method, containing videos of real-world scenarios captured under various conditions. Experimental results demonstrate the proposed method's superiority over existing approaches, outperforming them in terms of accuracy and reliability. Furthermore, it can be adapted to different applications with minimal fine-tuning and can provide consistent results in new, unseen data. This research introduces a novel, multi-task sequence prediction system grounded in recurrent neural networks that tackles the complex task of annotating TUN-ARABI, a variety of Tunisian Arabizi, at multiple levels of annotation simultaneously. The performance of algebraic multigrid (AMG) methods heavily relies on the efficiency of the smoothing phase, which typically employs Gaussian elimination for linear systems. In many cases, applying Gaussian elimination results in significant computational delays when dealing with large, sparse linear equations, common in many numerical analysis applications. This paper explores a method of reducing the computational complexity of Gaussian elimination to achieve time-efficient solutions for these systems, particularly in numerical PDE-based AMG methods. We demonstrate the feasibility of using this approach within an AMG framework to obtain substantial reductions in smoothing phase times, potentially leading to improved overall performance. Experimental validation of this strategy is provided through various numerical tests, showcasing its benefits and applicability. Moreover, this approach can be easily combined with other optimization strategies to enhance its effectiveness. Code for this strategy is included in an open-source AMG library, which can be accessed on the associated GitHub repository. Additionally, a brief introduction to numerical PDE-based AMG methods is provided for readers who are unfamiliar with the subject. In real-world environments, classifying data often encounters the challenge of
working with small datasets. Transfer learning has been proven effective in this
scenario by leveraging knowledge from similar tasks to improve classification
performance in tasks with limited data. However, traditional transfer learning
methods often fail to account for the differences in data distributions across
tasks, leading to suboptimal results. This paper introduces an innovative
approach to transfer learning that focuses on adapting the data distribution of
source tasks to that of the target task, using a technique called Maximum
Mean Displacement (MMD). Experimental results on multiple datasets show that
this approach achieves better performance than existing state-of-the-art methods. 
A notable advantage of our approach is its ability to handle multiple source
tasks, which is not possible with existing methods. The code for this method is
made available on GitHub. 
\textbf{https://github.com/abdo20/MMD-TL} 
We also provide a code for a baseline method that uses pre-trained models and
domain adaptation techniques. 
\textbf{https://github.com/abdo20/TL-Baseline}. 
All the code is written in Python and utilizes the PyTorch library. The paper
includes an analysis of the trade-offs between different hyperparameters used in
our approach. We also explore the effect of using different feature spaces on
our approach's performance.

Our results demonstrate that these algorithms can effectively provide deterministic performance in these networks, and we discuss the implications of these findings for future research and development. Distributed representations in computational linguistics allow for the transfer of models across languages, making it easier to apply existing knowledge to new languages. However, the representations used in such models can be sensitive to the specific corpus used to train them and may not generalize effectively to new data. This paper explores the potential of using representations that combine word meanings with etymological connections that are common across multiple languages, thereby enhancing their ability to withstand variations in word ordering and out-of-vocabulary words. We demonstrate that etymologically-constrained embeddings exhibit greater robustness than standard BERT-based embeddings when evaluated on out-of-domain language tasks, such as predicting word similarities and distinguishing between synonyms and antonyms. Additionally, our etymologically-constrained embeddings outperform BERT-based embeddings on in-domain tasks, such as identifying semantic relations in text. We also provide insights into the linguistic insights that can be gleaned from these etymologically-constrained embeddings. Our code and data are available for download at https://github.com/salesilva/etc-embeddings. Furthermore, we have made our etymological resources available to the public, including a database of language family trees, the etymological connections between English words, and the language links in the Universal Dependencies dataset, known as UNIY. These resources can be accessed at https://github.com/salesilva/etymological-resources. The language links in the UNIY database can be used to create etymologically-constrained embeddings for any language tree without requiring the corresponding word vectors. We have released a Python API to access this data, making it easy to use in various projects. Our models and results can be reproduced using the EtcPy library, available on GitHub at https://github.com/salesilva/etc.py. The etymological connections used to create the UNIY links are based on the 2020 update of the Digital Library of etymological connections, known as DLE. The DLE database contains over 1.5 billion word connections across 1.5 billion etymological links, covering 1.5 billion etymological links across 2.5 billion word connections. The DLE database is available for download at https://dle.diccionario.com/. Our etymological embeddings are also compatible with the 2020 update of the Digital Lexicon of Indo-European roots by Baldi (2020). This paper introduces Learned Bloom Filters, a new data structure that leverages Neural Networks to enhance efficiency, while also allowing for inverse operations. By combining the efficiency of neural networks with the advantages of Bloom Filters, Learned Bloom Filters offer a promising solution to real-world problems. This concept is further explored in the context of Learned Decision Filters, which utilize a neural network to determine optimal decisions by selecting the $k$ most promising elements from a predefined set. By modeling the decision process as a sequence of independent choices, Learned Decision Filters can be implemented using Learned Bloom Filters to achieve high performance. To illustrate the efficacy of this approach, several concrete examples are developed, including a dynamic programming solution to shortest paths, linear programming, and the 0/1-Knapsack problem. Experimental results confirm that Learned Decision Filters can outperform traditional methods, with significant performance gains achievable. For instance, on the Enron Email Dataset, Learned Decision Filters offer a $3.5$ to $5$ times speedup over existing methods, with a comparable level of accuracy. In Cloud Computing, the embedding of virtual networks within underlying infrastructures is formalized as the Virtual Network Embedding (VNE) issue. A key challenge in this field is the dynamic allocation of virtual resources to reduce costs. A new approach, leveraging a two-stage method, is proposed to tackle VNE. In the first stage, a genetic algorithm is applied to embed virtual connections within a graph model. In the second stage, residual graphs are generated based on the allocated connections, and a genetic algorithm is used to embed virtual machines on the available nodes of these graphs. Our approach was evaluated in comparison to existing methods, demonstrating its effectiveness in reducing node and link delays on real-world topologies. Music streaming platforms provide three main ways to access and listen to content: searching for specific tracks, browsing through albums, and discovering related songs. While these modes of interaction are well understood for traditional music stores, their effectiveness when combined in a streaming context has not been thoroughly studied. This study examines the influence of search, browsing, and recommendation on content access behavior using real user interaction data from a leading music streaming platform. We will describe the data used, the preprocessing steps taken, and present the results, also discussing how our findings can be applied in practice. Our analysis reveals that content access behavior is influenced by the time of day, day of the week, and specific weeks within the month, indicating that users' preferences vary over different time scales. We also found that certain users tend to use one mode of interaction more than others, and that combining all modes leads to more content access. Furthermore, our research shows that content access due to search, browsing, and recommendation are highly correlated, and that users' preferences for specific content are influenced by the way they interact with the platform. We also found that the effectiveness of search, browsing, and recommendation in terms of content access grows as users spend more time interacting with the platform. These findings can be used to optimize content recommendation systems, improve user experience, and enhance platform interactions. We believe that this research can serve as a valuable guide for future studies on content access and recommendation in a streaming context. We also provide a theoretical framework that generalizes OT to handle large and heterogeneous collections of datasets, setting the stage for new statistical challenges and opportunities in this area. The search for neutrinoless double-beta decay is a crucial method in determining whether neutrinos possess mass. To achieve this goal, researchers require an enormous number of isoscalar electrons to detect within a highly background-free environment. A potential solution to this challenge is the use of liquid argon, a scintillator that exhibits excellent light yield and can track electromagnetic showers with precision. A study conducted to investigate liquid argon's suitability for this purpose involved exposing it to beta particles and gamma rays, resulting in an observed light yield of 0.75 +/- 0.03 (stat) +/- 0.10 (syst) pe/MeV for beta particles and 0.25 +/- 0.02 (stat) +/- 0.02 (syst) pe/MeV for gamma rays. These results correspond to an effective energy threshold of 350 keV for neutrinoless double-beta decay in liquid argon, significantly higher than that of traditional scintillators. Notably, this study employed a liquid argon detector with an advanced micropixel photon detector, capable of mapping light signals with high spatial resolution. Our findings demonstrate the potential of liquid argon as a viable scintillator for neutrinoless double-beta decay experiments. Ultimately, this approach could enable researchers to achieve background levels competitive with current facilities, albeit at the cost of reduced energy resolution, which must be considered in the overall assessment. Additional studies are required to further investigate the subject matter. A conceptual design for a liquid argon detector utilizing a micropixel photon detector is presented, featuring a 10-ton liquid argon active mass and 360 square meters of surface area. Our simulation results suggest that such a detector could achieve a background level of 0.1 events / (ton-year)/(keV) at an energy threshold of 100 keV, rivaling the current status of experiments like the Majorana Demonstrator. This research represents the first successful measurement of light yield in liquid argon, opening the door for further studies of neutrinoless double-beta decay. Our findings also underscore the potential of micropixel photon detectors in enabling high-precision imaging of liquid argon, a crucial aspect of scintillation detection. As such, this study is a significant step towards the development of large-scale liquid argon detectors for future neutrinoless double-beta decay experiments. Our results indicate that such detectors could achieve background levels competitive with current facilities, provided that improvements in energy resolution are addressed. As the use of machine learning algorithms expands, there is a growing concern about their potential biases. Fair representation learning aims to eliminate these biases by creating a representation that fairly encapsulates diverse groups within a population. However, current methods often fail to generalize to new data points, effectively reducing their effectiveness to a sophisticated data smoothing technique. In contrast, we propose that a fair representation should prioritize capturing underlying patterns in the data, rather than surface-level variations. To achieve this, we introduce a fair representation learning approach that targets specific attributes and promotes a more robust and generalizable representation. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach can be successfully applied to various data sets to produce a representation that fairly represents the data. Furthermore, we show that this representation can be used to improve the performance of downstream tasks, such as classification. The code supporting our findings is publicly available on GitHub, accessible at https://github.com/automl/FairLearn. An independent implementation of our approach can also be found at https://nsoi2.github.io/FairLearn. The research was partially supported by a Google Research Grant. Our focus was on stars with high ratios of europium to magnesium, which indicate a significant contribution of rare r-process elements from external sources. We identified 69 stars with elevated europium levels and investigated their origins. A significant number of these stars are likely the remnants of smaller galaxies that merged with the Milky Way, which is consistent with previous findings. However, our results also suggest that some of these stars could be the stripped halos of these merged galaxies. A smaller group of stars with elevated europium levels may be the result of globular clusters, which are still debated as potential origin sources. A few stars with extremely high europium levels are either the remnants of ancient, metal-poor star-forming events or the result of unusual star formation processes. Our findings highlight the importance of studying the origins of rare element contributions to understanding the formation and evolution of the Milky Way. We also recommend further investigation into the contribution of globular clusters, mergers, and stripped halos to these contributions. Deep learning techniques have shown great potential in processing three-dimensional point cloud data, but their performance often relies heavily on access to extensive labeled data. This issue can be particularly challenging in certain applications where collecting sufficient training data proves difficult. In contrast, we propose an innovative approach that leverages synthetic data derived from three-dimensional objects to facilitate point cloud classification without relying on time-consuming annotation of real-world data. This method utilizes a generative adversarial network to create point cloud data that effectively captures the distribution of real-world data, enabling the development of a point cloud classifier. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by improving the state-of-the-art performance of a baseline point cloud classifier by 7.9% and 12.1% on the S3DIS dataset and ScanNet dataset, respectively. Furthermore, our method proves to be efficient, achieving a 2.5 fold speed increase in data generation time over the current state-of-the-art approach. Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) agents have achieved significant advancements in complex tasks, yet they often struggle with adapting to unexpected situations. Most existing research focuses on learning from data collected during training and exploration, but it neglects the implicit knowledge gained from pre-trained models. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach, called Pretrained Implicit Knowledge distillation (PIKD), which leverages pre-trained models' knowledge to guide the learning of a new DRL agent. This process involves two stages: initial exploration where the agent acquires experience and a model selector is created, and implicit knowledge distillation where the new agent is trained using the pre-trained model's knowledge and the model selector. The model selector and the implicit knowledge distillation process are implemented as two separate distillation tasks, enabling the agent to learn from two distinct sources of knowledge: explicit (exploratory experience) and implicit (pre-trained model's knowledge), resulting in improved performance. Experiments conducted on Atari games demonstrate the effectiveness of PIKD, which achieves state-of-the-art results for Deep Q-Networks (DQN) and Deep Deterministic Gradient Policy (DDPG) in multiple games. Notably, PIKD with DQN exhibits a substantial improvement of 9.1% in average score over the baseline DQN, and 5.1% with DDPG. The code is publicly available on GitHub. The future of computing heavily relies on the advancement of parallelization techniques. 
Existing parallelization tools struggle with code analysis and limited design frameworks, 
leading to poorly optimized code for high-performance computing.
To overcome these challenges, a new approach called aegir was developed, combining 
a comprehensive domain-specific language with innovative tools for code creation, 
optimization, and verification.
Aegir employs a revolutionary, graph-based programming model that seamlessly 
integrates parallelization technology and scales efficiently to millions of cores.
Its unique programming model and optimization tools enable efficient code generation 
for various platforms, including GPUs, while its verification capabilities ensure precise 
execution without memory errors.
As a result, aegir provides superior performance capabilities, demonstrated by its 
superiority in outperforming state-of-the-art libraries like cuBLAS in matrix-matrix 
multiplication, as well as its impressive speedup of 18.8x compared to a hand-optimized 
implementation of FFT.
These impressive results demonstrate that aegir can efficiently scale up to large 
problem sizes and outperform existing libraries, opening doors to new opportunities 
in high-performance computing. The code and tools developed with aegir are now open 
to the public, paving the way for further innovation and advancement in the field.

We introduce a novel neural network architecture for processing three-dimensional graph structures formed by atoms in 3D space. Our design ensures that the network remains agnostic to graph coordinates and unchanging patterns, and incorporates symmetry properties to preserve rotational invariance. The proposed architecture is based on message-passing neural networks, and we demonstrate its effectiveness through several case studies, including a proof-of-concept using a simple neural potential, and more advanced machine learning models for simulating the properties of amorphous and crystalline materials. Notably, our approach achieves state-of-the-art results in predicting elastic moduli of amorphous silicon, surpassing previous methods, and accurately models the elastic moduli of crystalline silicon without the need for training on crystal data. The accompanying code is publicly available on GitHub. Our research paves the way for the development of more advanced machine learning models capable of handling larger, more complex systems and providing more accurate predictions. We believe that this approach will be particularly beneficial for simulating the properties of amorphous materials and contributing to the advancement of machine learning-based atomistic simulations. Ultimately, our work has the potential to facilitate the design of innovative materials with tailored properties, such as improved thermal resistance or reduced electrical conductivity, by leveraging the power of machine learning. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/stephentromp/RAKE-MPNN. Given the complexity of the problem, we anticipate that further advancements will be necessary to achieve optimal results, and we encourage the machine learning and materials science communities to collaborate on this exciting challenge. In the context of continuum-armed bandit problems, researchers investigate a scenario where multiple arms, each associated with a single optimal value, are selected by an algorithm to minimize regret. Building on prior work, novel algorithms are proposed to address this challenge. These algorithms leverage a given level of confidence to define a range of potential optimal values and, using a piecewise linear function, create a family of metareward functions, each of which is bounded above and convex. By employing a standard multi-armed bandit algorithm to learn the metareward function, the optimal value can be approximated efficiently. Additionally, the concept of monotonicity is introduced, enabling more rapid learning when the metareward functions exhibit this property. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms in terms of reduced regret. The algorithms' applicability extends to real-world applications such as continuous-time recommendation systems, where optimal arm values correspond to optimal user preferences. In this setting, the algorithms are also applied to a dynamic user preference scenario, where optimal arm values must adapt to changing user preferences, resulting in improved regret compared to a naive approach. A key component in deep learning training is stochastic optimization, 
notably the stochastic gradient descent (SGD) algorithm, which has been 
improved by incorporating various techniques such as gradient clipping, 
quantization, and mixed precision arithmetic to enhance performance without 
fully understanding their underlying principles. This study delves into the 
behavior of a novel variant of SGD, known as the batch-size-augmented SGD, 
which leverages critical batch sizes to attain superior generalization-distribution 
generalization performance. By analyzing the batch-size-augmented SGD using 
mean-field large deviation theory, we establish that it converges to a specific 
stationary distribution under mild conditions, providing insights into its 
behavior. We demonstrate that this variant exhibits a two-stage convergence 
process, transitioning from an initial local minimum to the stationary distribution 
while outperforming standard SGD in terms of generalization performance. 
Furthermore, we derive a novel generalization bound for batch-size-augmented 
SGD, highlighting its potential to achieve superior results with a critical 
batch size, which can lead to significant improvements in generalization 
performance. Finally, we validate these findings through comprehensive 
experiments on various deep learning models. The results show that 
batch-size-augmented SGD consistently outperforms standard SGD, 
particularly when using a critical batch size, achieving superior generalization 
performance with substantial speedups, reaching orders of magnitude in some cases. 
This breakthrough has significant implications for large-scale deep learning 
training, potentially enabling generalization performance to be improved with 
increased computational power. We believe that these findings can contribute 
to better understanding of SGD and inform the development of more effective 
optimization algorithms for deep learning applications. The code and models used 
in this research can be accessed at https://github.com/alexsmisina/batch_size_augmented_sgd. 
A companion paper, also published on arXiv, provides a more detailed theoretical 
analysis of the batch-size-augmented SGD algorithm. The arXiv paper can be found 
at https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.13070. The implementation is also available on 
PyTorch, along with a research paper, at https://github.com/alexsmisina/batch_size_augmented_sgd_pytorch. 
Additional information about the research, including a blog, can be found 
at https://batchsizeaugmentedsgd.github.io.

By drawing inspiration from recent advances in mutual information estimators, we develop a theoretical framework for interpreting distillation as a method for estimating mutual information. Through a combination of theoretical analysis and empirical testing, we demonstrate that this perspective offers insights into the effectiveness of various distillation techniques. Specifically, we find that some commonly used methods are more effective when they align with the underlying mutual information structure, while others are less effective when they do not. By applying this framework to a variety of benchmark datasets, we provide evidence that it is a valuable tool for understanding and improving knowledge distillation. These findings suggest that low-energy nuclear emulsions can be highly effective in detecting light forces, particularly for particles with masses below 140 MeV.  Additionally, it is found that nuclear emulsions can be highly sensitive to dark matter that interacts via light forces, offering a competitive detection capability to current experiments.  Finally, it is concluded that future nuclear emulsion detectors, such as the P-ONE experiment, have great potential in detecting light forces and could potentially discover new particles with high significance. Recent advancements in autonomous driving systems have led to the development of sophisticated systems that can navigate complex traffic environments. To ensure the safety of these systems, it is crucial to test and evaluate them using diverse scenarios generated by generative models. This paper proposes an approach to create adversarial situations that can challenge autonomous driving systems. By combining a latent code with a pre-trained model of the system, it uses an inverse dynamics generator to produce a sequence of control inputs that can cause the system to deviate from its intended path. To improve the adversarial scenario generation process, a conditional GAN is trained using a combination of real-world and manipulated scenarios. Additionally, a method is proposed to guide the generation process using a gradient-based optimization technique. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach, revealing that the generated adversarial situations are indeed challenging for the model when it operates in non-stationary conditions. It is also shown that the proposed method outperforms existing approaches in terms of image quality and diversity. Finally, it is established that the use of a pre-trained model significantly enhances the robustness of the generated adversarial situations. This research is part of an ongoing project aimed at creating a comprehensive evaluation framework for autonomous driving systems. Future work will involve integrating this approach into the evaluation framework and conducting experiments to assess its effectiveness. A crucial step in the Structure-from-Motion process involves obtaining camera positions by analyzing 2D feature correlations across multiple images. This challenge is addressed by Structure-from-Motion pipelines using multiple views, as they attempt to determine camera positions based on 3D scene points, despite such a task being highly underdetermined. To address this issue, researchers have developed various methods, including RANSAC-like algorithms and photometric bundle adjustment, which optimize camera positions by iteratively adjusting the camera poses and 3D scene geometry until a coherent 3D model is obtained. This study presents a new, efficient optimization method that combines 2D feature correlations and camera poses to obtain a single coherent 3D model. The method iteratively optimizes camera poses and 3D scene points, utilizing the scene's geometry to refine feature correspondences, and vice versa. Through rigorous testing on synthetic and real-world datasets, our approach demonstrated superior performance over existing methods, including its own iteration. The code used for this research is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/avito260/SMR. In the field of artificial intelligence, particularly in computer science, games serve as a key benchmark for measuring the capabilities of various algorithms. A notable example is the OpenAI Five program, which successfully dominated every major chess opponent through its advanced multi-agent approach. This paper introduces a new game called Open Scavenger, derived from King of Thumb, a traditional board game, and designed to be played by multiple AI agents. By analyzing the game's properties, we found that it presents a challenging environment for traditional planning algorithms, with a high level of complexity due to its high branching factors. To address this issue, we developed a heuristic planning approach that utilizes a custom evaluation function, resulting in significantly more efficient planning times - approximately 0.6 seconds per plan. Our implementation successfully integrated with DeepMind's Unity robotics environment and allowed for seamless robot control. Additionally, we achieved notable results in a multi-agent version of the game, with a significant lead over traditional single-agent planning algorithms, demonstrating the potential of our approach for use in robotics.
